aiSystem.title: Does the system infer, from the input it receives, predictions, content, recommendations or decisions, with some level of autonomy?
aiSystem.why: Only AI systems within the meaning of Art. 3(1) fall under the Regulation. Software that only applies rules defined by people is not one (recital 12).
aiSystem.example1: Yes: a trained model that scores applications.
aiSystem.example2: No: a hand-written calculation grid in a spreadsheet.

scope.title: Does the system fall under an exclusion of the Regulation?
scope.why: Art. 2 excludes some uses from the scope of the Regulation. One exclusion is enough.
scope.example1: A model developed and used for scientific research only.
scope.example2: A tool used for purely personal, non-professional purposes.

options.military: Exclusively military, defence or national security use (Art. 2(3))
options.research: Developed and put into service for scientific research only (Art. 2(6))
options.testing: Research, testing or development before any placing on the market (Art. 2(8))
options.thirdCountry: Used by a third-country authority under international cooperation (Art. 2(4))

prohibited.title: Does the system implement any of these practices?
prohibited.why: Art. 5 prohibits some practices in every sector. They cannot be remedied: they must stop.
prohibited.example1: Inferring employees' emotions during a performance review.
prohibited.example2: Assigning a social score that leads to unrelated detrimental treatment.

options.a: Subliminal or manipulative techniques distorting behaviour (a)
options.b: Exploiting vulnerabilities due to age, disability or social situation (b)
options.c: Social scoring leading to detrimental treatment (c)
options.d: Predicting offences based solely on profiling (d)
options.f: Emotion recognition in the workplace or in education (f)
options.h: Real-time remote biometric identification by law enforcement in public spaces (h)

annexI.title: Is the system a safety component of an Annex I product subject to third-party assessment?
annexI.why: Art. 6(1) classifies as high risk the safety components of products covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation (medical devices, machinery, toys…).
annexI.example1: Yes: the AI module that detects an anomaly in a medical device.
annexI.example2: No: HR software, which is not an Annex I product.

annexIII.title: Is the system used for any of these use cases?
annexIII.why: Annex III lists the high-risk use cases (Art. 6(2)). Tick all that apply; in most cases none does.
annexIII.example1: Sorting or filtering job applications: point 4(a).
annexIII.example2: Assessing a person's creditworthiness: point 5(b) (fraud detection is excluded).

options.3(c): 3(c) Assessment of the appropriate level of education
options.4(a): 4(a) Recruitment and selection: job ad targeting, filtering, candidate evaluation
options.4(b): 4(b) Worker management: promotion, termination, task allocation based on personal traits, performance monitoring
options.5(a): 5(a) Eligibility for public benefits and services
options.5(b): 5(b) Creditworthiness and credit scoring (excluding fraud detection)
options.5(c): 5(c) Risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance
options.6(b): 6(b) Law enforcement: polygraphs and similar tools
options.6(d): 6(d) Law enforcement: risk of offending or reoffending
options.7(c): 7(c) Migration: examination of asylum, visa and residence applications
options.8(b): 8(b) Influencing an election or voting behaviour

profiling.title: Does the system profile natural persons?
profiling.why: Profiling (automated evaluation of personal aspects: work performance, economic situation, behaviour…) makes the system high risk even if an Art. 6(3) condition is met (Art. 6(3), last subparagraph).
profiling.example1: Yes: ranking candidates by a relevance score for the job.
profiling.example2: No: extracting the name and experience from a CV without scoring them.

art63.title: Is the system limited to one of these tasks?
art63.why: Art. 6(3) rules out high risk when the system does not materially influence the decision. This position is documented before placing on the market (Art. 6(4)).
art63.example1: A narrow procedural task: extracting CV fields, proposing interview slots.
art63.example2: A preparatory task: translating the documents of a file before a person reviews it.

options.b: Improving the result of a previously completed human activity (b)
options.c: Detecting decision patterns or deviations, without replacing human assessment (c)

transparency.title: Does the system interact with people or generate content?
transparency.why: Art. 50 requires informing people who interact with an AI system and marking synthetic content. These obligations apply since 2 August 2026.
transparency.example2: An image or synthetic voice generator.

options.generatesSyntheticContent: It generates synthetic text, images, audio or video

developer.title: Did your company develop this system, or have it developed to place it on the market under its own name?
developer.why: The provider (Art. 3(3)) bears most obligations; the deployer (Art. 3(4)) uses a system under its own authority.
developer.example1: Yes: your team trained the scoring model built into your product.
developer.example2: No: you use an ATS bought from a vendor.

art25.title: Have you done any of the following to a third-party system?
art25.why: Art. 25(1) makes you the provider of a high-risk system if you put your brand on it, substantially modify it or change its intended purpose.
art25.example1: Reselling under your brand a scoring tool bought from a vendor.
art25.example2: Repurposing a general-purpose chatbot to screen applications.

options.ownBrand: Putting your name or trademark on it (Art. 25(1)(a))
options.substantialModification: Substantially modifying it, for example retraining it (Art. 25(1)(b))

packVerify.body:
# Verifying this audit pack

This pack is verified without a ProofLayer account and without network access. The command `npx @prooflayer/verify pack.zip` runs the six steps below and exits with code 0 (no tampering) or 1. They can also be redone by hand, with `openssl` and `sha256sum`.

## 1. Manifest signature

`manifest.json` is signed with Ed25519 by key `{kid}`. The signed bytes are the canonical JSON form (RFC 8785) of the manifest without its `signature` field. ProofLayer's public keys are published at {keysUrl} and pinned in the verification tool.

## 2. File integrity

The manifest lists every file in the pack with its SHA-256 hash (`files`). Example: `sha256sum report.pdf`.

## 3. Disclosed evidence

Each `evidence/<id>.json` file holds the payload, salt and envelope of one item of evidence. Recompute `contentSha256 = SHA-256(JCS(payload))` then `leafHash = SHA-256(0x00 ‖ salt ‖ JCS(envelope))`, the envelope being `{{ v, org, id, kind, sourceRef, occurredAt, capturedAt, contentSha256, attachmentSha256 }}`. Any attachment hashes to `attachmentSha256`.

## 4. Batches

Each `proofs/batches/<seq>.json` file lists ALL the leaves of the batch, disclosed or not: an omitted item remains visible through its `leafHash` alone. The Merkle root (RFC 6962) of the leaves must equal `header.merkleRoot`, and `SHA-256(JCS(header))` must equal `batchHash`. Batches follow each other without gaps and each `prevBatchHash` is the `batchHash` of the previous batch.

## 5. Anchors and timestamps

Each `proofs/anchors/<seq>.json` file lists the anchor's `batchHash` values; their root must equal `header.merkleRoot`, and `SHA-256(JCS(header))` must equal `anchorHash`. The RFC 3161 token timestamps `anchorHash`:

    openssl ts -verify -digest <anchorHash> -in proofs/anchors/<seq>.tst -token_in -CAfile proofs/tsa/<provider>.pem

## 6. Census

The manifest states the number of leaves in the period, the number of disclosed items and the difference. A batch without an anchor (`anchor: null`) has not yet been timestamped by the provider.

## What sealing proves

The content of an item of evidence existed no later than the token date and has not changed since; no item has been removed from a batch; the order of batches is intact. It does not prove that the event happened in the source tool: each item carries its source address for cross-checking. Declarative evidence (uploaded document, attestation) dates the upload, not the truth of the document.

publicVerify.title: Verify an audit pack
publicVerify.intro: Drop a ProofLayer audit pack (.zip file) to check that no evidence has been changed, removed or backdated since it was sealed.
publicVerify.privacy: The file never leaves your device: verification runs entirely in your browser, nothing is sent to ProofLayer.
publicVerify.notZip: This file is not a .zip archive.

verdict.okWithWarnings: No alteration, with points to note

verdictText.ok: All disclosed evidence matches its sealed hash, and every timestamp is valid.
verdictText.okWithWarnings: No evidence has been changed. Some elements cannot be established, however: see the details below.
verdictText.fail: At least one element of the pack no longer matches what was sealed. Do not rely on this pack without an explanation from its issuer.

signature.title: Pack signature
signature.what: The manifest is signed by ProofLayer, and every file in the pack matches its listed hash.

evidence.title: Disclosed evidence
evidence.what: Each evidence item is recomputed from its content and found at its place in its sealed batch.

batches.title: Evidence batches
batches.what: Each batch is intact and batches follow each other without gaps: no evidence has been removed.

anchors.title: Anchors
anchors.what: Each batch is included in a shared anchor, timestamped by a third party.

timestamps.title: Third-party timestamp
timestamps.what: The timestamp token (RFC 3161) is signed by a recognised provider and dates the anchor.

census.title: Census
census.what: The number of evidence items in the period, disclosed or not, matches what the pack states.

publicVerify.proves: What verification establishes: the content of each evidence item existed no later than the timestamp date and has not changed since; no evidence has been removed from a batch; the order of batches is intact. It does not establish that the event happened in the source tool, nor that an uploaded document is truthful.
publicVerify.cli: Same verification on the command line: npx @prooflayer/verify pack.zip
